synopsis: Cloud execution rents computing capacity by the hour for parallel simulations, matching bursty demand that could otherwise leave purchased machines idle; vendor clouds run particular simulators, while generic clouds rent raw machines [f16057, f16058, f16059, f16061]. Quoted 2026 public rates include AWS g6e.xlarge with one L40S at about USD 1.861/hour, eight-L40S capacity at USD 30.131/hour, and Google g2-standard-32 with one L4 at USD 1.734/hour; a one-year AWS commitment lowers the single-L40S rate to about USD 1.17/hour [f8855, f8858, f8861, f8859]. Spot capacity suits checkpointable regression rather than deterministic HIL or irreplaceable long jobs, and its quoted AWS prices vary widely between trackers [f8864, f8860]. Compute is described as cheap relative to engineering labor, but the four-month window limits throughput: ten single-processor instances running continuously for 122 days cost roughly USD 54,000 and provide at most about 29,000 processor-hours [f16070, f16071]. Public prices were not found for the named simulator-vendor clouds, and vendor terms, export controls and data residency were not researched; sensitive site scans, mine layouts and machine CAD motivate an on-premises or private-cloud option [f9256, f16068, f16069]. Procurement should price concurrent workers and cloud rights rather than desktop seats alone, recheck regional prices, and address capacity constraints with multi-region planning, justified reservations and a local fallback [f16486, f8865, f8925, f8926].
